summary: This memo discusses the role of gateways in an internetwork, especially the trouble of translating between different protocol suites. It points to mismatched functions, routing bottlenecks, flow control problems, and the high cost of translating gateways. Originally a MITRE Corporation report, it is a discussion paper.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine two towns speaking different languages with one translator in the middle. If the translator is slow or confused, everyone suffers, so this memo asks whether that is a good idea.

questions: why are protocol translating gateways a problem
what is the addressing problem in gateways
subtitle: Why protocol translating gateways between different networks cause deep problems.

tldr.problem: System architects casually propose gateways to connect networks with different protocol suites, assuming they solve interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: M.A. Padlipsky shows that translating or mapping gateways face irresolvable functionality mismatches (addressing, out-of-band signals, flow control), state management problems, and become bottlenecks that cannot be replicated or updated easily.
tldr.outcome: The paper argues that building protocol-compatible internets with a single suite is preferable, and that architects who propose gateways often underestimate complexity.

today: RFC 875 reflects early 1980s concerns about protocol translation. The Internet converged on a single protocol suite (TCP/IP), validating the paper's preference for protocol-compatible networks. Modern issues of protocol translation and gateway complexity persist when connecting heterogeneous systems, but the Internet standard avoids the multi-protocol gateway problem.

sections.title: The Gateway Problem
sections.content:
RFC 875 is an opinion piece from M.A. Padlipsky arguing that system architects routinely propose translating or mapping gateways (T/MGs) to connect networks with different protocol suites without understanding the deep problems such designs create.

The author notes that the ARPANET research community explicitly decided it would be too hard to gateway networks whose protocols differed above the host-to-communications-subnetwork-processor level. ARPANET gateways assume all attached networks share the same host-host protocol (TCP/IP) and process-level protocols. This constraint exists because translating between different protocol sets creates irresolvable problems.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC warns that connecting networks that speak different protocol languages is much harder than architects realize.

sections.title: The Addressing Mismatch
sections.content:
The most significant problem is host addressing. NCP-using networks have one-dimensional addresses: a single Host field in the Host-IMP leader gets exhausted when the field fills. IP uses two-dimensional addressing: a network field and a host field, allowing far more flexibility. To gateway between NCP and TCP networks, you must somehow express a foreign network address in an NCP message, but NCP has no mechanism for this.

Workarounds exist: using spare bits in headers, changing the Initial Connection Protocol, or sending the internet address as data. But all workarounds require changing the pre-existing protocols. Since accepting protocol changes defeats the entire purpose of gatewaying incompatible networks, you are left with no practical solution.

One alternative is a Janus Host (a gateway that terminates NCP as an application on one side and initiates TCP on the other), but this confers extremely limited functionality and only works for user-initiated connections like Telnet, not for background transfers like FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: NCP networks say a Host is number 5. TCP networks say Host 5 is on network 3. The translator does not know how to tell NCP about network 3.

sections.title: Flow Control and State Problems
sections.content:
NCP follows a discipline where hosts wait for RFNM (Ready For Next Message) from the IMP before sending more data. When gatewaying through a T/MG, the RFNM comes from the T/MG's own IMP, not the true destination. The T/MG must buffer extensively to bridge this mismatch, and in worst cases the foreign network might provide no feedback mechanism at all without protocol changes.

Out-of-band signals present another mismatch. NCP uses Interrupt commands on a control link. TCP uses an Urgent bit in message headers. These semantics differ significantly. If you need Urgent to signal a virtual quit button, it must cause the process to take special action, not merely alert the protocol interpreter. When a T/MG receives an NCP Interrupt and has only TCP Expedited Data to forward, it cannot preserve the semantics.

Replicating a T/MG creates a state management crisis. Each open logical connection carries state information maintained by its T/MG. A second T/MG has no access to that state, so connections cannot migrate between gateways. This makes it nearly impossible to replicate gateways for reliability or load distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway must remember which messages came from where. If two gateways try to share the work, they step on each other.

sections.title: Additional Technical Challenges
sections.content:
Moving target problems emerge whenever protocols change. If you have built multiple T/MGs for different protocol pair combinations, and then one protocol is revised, all affected T/MGs must be redesigned. Given that SNA has seen three versions, DECNET likewise, and ISO continues to define additional layers, the maintenance burden becomes prohibitive.

The NCP-to-TCP example also illustrates problems at the application level. NCP mail (using FTP) identifies destinations by name because the Host is determined by the Host-Host Protocol. TCP requires a full host address specification. The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (RFC 788) required 62 pages to specify this single point of translation.

Complexity scales dramatically with protocol distance. NCP and TCP have an evolutionary relationship and nominally shared process-level protocols, yet bridging them is painful. Moving between completely different suites like DECNET, SNA, or incomplete NBS/ISO protocols would require far more powerful T/MGs.
sections.plainLanguage: When protocols change, the translator must change too. Translating between networks that are completely different costs much more than a small change.

sections.title: The Heffalump Trap
sections.content:
The RFC uses a Winnie-the-Pooh metaphor to explain why architects propose T/MGs despite their difficulty. Pooh makes a Heffalump Trap by digging a pit and baiting it with honey, but when he goes to retrieve the honey he gets his head stuck in a jar and becomes the monster Piglet feared to trap.

Similarly, architects casually propose T/MGs in block diagrams without understanding what they are building. Sometimes this is pure buzzwording: contractors seek contracts by promising ambitious solutions with impressive-sounding names. But often it reflects ignorance of the oral tradition of why the ARPANET community explicitly rejected this approach.

The RFC concludes that system architects who propose T/MGs have not done their homework. Like the Heffalump, which nobody had actually seen, the T/MG is something everyone talks about without understanding it. The practical lesson: protocol-compatible internets using a single protocol suite are far preferable to translating gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Architects hear about gateways but do not really understand them, like Pooh hearing about Heffalumps. They draw gateways in their plans without knowing how hard they are to build.
